content_list.content_text: The '70s were a fertile era for horror. Subversive, nihilistic, shockingly immediate with its camera vérité, George A. Romero's (b. 1940) apocalyptic zombie film Night of the Living Dead (1968) suggested that something was very wrong in the United States, and a new generation of filmmakers didn't exactly want to continue the earlier work, preferring to scorch the whole territory.

information.contentText: Carrie is one of the few horror films to be nominated for several Academy Awards. Spacek and Laurie received nominations for Best Actress and Best Supporting Actress, respectively. The film also won the grand prize at the Avoriaz Film Festival, while Spacek received the Best Actress award from the National Society of Film Critics. In 2008, Carrie was ranked number 86 on Empire magazine's list of The 500 Greatest Movies of All Time. The film also made Entertainment Weekly's list of the 50 best high school movies, and its final sequence (better known as the "prom scene") was named one of the 100 scariest moments of all time.

content_list.content_text: "You watch these films and you know you're in the hands of a maniac," said John Landis (b. 1950), referring to the dangerous and singular output of Wes Craven (b. 1939), David Cronenberg (b. 1943), Brian De Palma (b. 1940), David Lynch (b. 1946), and John Carpenter (b. 1948). This was a new breed of creators, influenced by films such as Psycho (1960) and Rosemary's Baby (1968), as well as by the French New Wave and the sociopolitical and economic situation of the time.

quote.quote: I was too young to know that I was being foolhardy when I demanded that we shoot the film in the Atlantic Ocean and not in a North Hollywood tank.
quote.author: Steven Spielberg on Jaws (1975)

content_list.content_text: "We're talking about bad karma - it's got to go somewhere," said Wes Craven, referring to Vietnam, the civil rights movement, feminism, the sexual revolution, the Kent State shootings, and the oil embargo. All of it ended up in an abundance of homemade, sensationalist films that obliterated the myth of the nuclear family and devoted themselves to the sick and the dispossessed.

content_list.title: The Resurrection of Monster Movies with Alien
content_list.description:
"In space no one can hear you scream." The tagline on the Alien poster was an obvious come-on, but there was plenty of screaming in theaters. Defying the popularity of Star Wars (1977), Ridley Scott (b. 1937) resurrected the cheap genre of scary monsters from outer space, paired it with a meticulous, big-budget look and created a paralyzing science fiction horror film capable of leaving nerves completely frayed.

Dan O'Bannon's sophisticated screenplay owes a great deal to the ingenious 1950s B movie Giant from the Unknown (1958) and follows the "haunted house" formula of The Cat and the Canary (1939) or Ten Little Indians (1965), but set aboard a spaceship and with a much greater gross-out factor.

The Nostromo is a gigantic cargo ship operating in deep space, with a minimal (and far from conventional) crew led by Captain Dallas (Tom Skerritt) that includes the smart Lieutenant Ripley (Sigourney Weaver) and Jones the cat. Responding to a distress call, they discover an abandoned alien ship and strange eggs. As they examine the eggs, a parasite leaps out of one and latches onto Kane's (John Hurt) helmet, infecting him and, a few days later, wreaking terrifying havoc when a baby alien bursts out of his chest during breakfast. The other actors supposedly didn't know what was going to happen, which made their shock and revulsion genuine.

Scott creates a frisson and uses the dark corridors dramatically as the dwindling crew - who apparently never watched a horror film as teenagers - walks straight into the monster's pair of extendable jaws. What raised the anguish to an art form, through Oscar-winning visual effects, was the unparalleled art direction and design, blending organic and metallic patterns, as well as the (only glimpsed) alien designed by the artist H. R. Giger, whose terrible beauty was given an eerie grace by the statuesque Maasai dancer Bolaji Badejo.

Weaver became a star and an icon overnight as the brave survivor Ripley, facing her final battle in nothing but a T-shirt and underwear. She was supposed to end the film naked, to emphasize human fragility in the face of the perfect killing machine, but 20th Century Fox, eager to avoid an "R" rating (restricted for those under 17) in the United States, vetoed the idea. Unusually for a horror franchise, the sequels were handed to directors famous for their distinctive visual styles - James Cameron, David Fincher and Jean-Pierre Jeunet.
content_list.credits: Summary based on the text by Angela Errigo, published in the book 1001 Movies You Must See Before You Die.

content_list.content_text: Even Britain jumped on the bandwagon, with the musty Hammer releasing a few pleasantly dark surprises - Demons of the Mind (1972) - during its prolonged death throes before the lights went out, and the fall of the houses of Tigon and Amicus welcoming the sadistic films of former porn director Peter Walker (b. 1939), such as House of Whipcord (1974).

information.contentText: The film was released in the United States on May 23, 1980, and in the United Kingdom on October 2, 1980, by Warner Bros. There were several versions for theatrical release, each shorter than the last; about 27 minutes were cut in total. Reactions to the film at the time of its release were mixed; Stephen King criticized the film for its deviations from the original novel. Assessment became more favorable in the following decades, and the work is now widely regarded as one of the greatest and most influential horror films ever made. The Shining is widely acclaimed by today's critics and has become a pop culture icon. In 2018, the film was selected for preservation in the National Film Registry by the Library of Congress as being "culturally, historically, or aesthetically significant." A sequel, Doctor Sleep, was released on November 8, 2019.

content_list.content_text: Meanwhile, an astonishing double bill was provided in 1973 by Don't Look Now (1973), a devastating study of grief and superstition by Nicolas Roeg (b. 1928), and The Wicker Man (1973), a sinister erotic and pagan nightmare set on a Scottish island.

quote.quote: I dreamed that I, that I killed you and Danny. But I didn't just kill you. I cut you up in little pieces. Oh my God. I must be losing my mind.
quote.author: Jack Torrance (Jack Nicholson) in The Shining (1980)

content_list.content_text: Rosemary's Baby paved the way for a number of scary films with religious themes. The most famous, The Exorcist (1973) and The Omen (1976), are examples of the trend toward producing horror films with big budgets and well-known stars.

information.contentText: The low-budget film caught the interest of producer Irvin Shapiro, who helped get it screened during the 1982 Cannes Film Festival. Horror novelist Stephen King gave The Evil Dead a good review, thereby convincing New Line Cinema to distribute the film. Although it had little commercial success in the United States, the film made back its budget through international distribution, grossing about $2.4 million during its theatrical run. Reviews of the film, both upon its release and in the years that followed, were universally positive, and The Evil Dead earned a reputation as one of the greatest cult films and is often described as one of the best horror films. Evil Dead launched the careers of Campbell and Raimi, who went on to collaborate on several films over the years, including the Spider-Man trilogy.

content_list.content_text: Jaws (1975) and Alien (1979) breathed new life into monster movies, while The Shining (1980) featured dazzling sets, extravagant production design, flawless technique and credits headed by names such as Jack Nicholson (b. 1937) and Stanley Kubrick (1928-1999).

content_list.title: The Horror Film Phenomenon
content_list.description:
This film, the first blockbuster in the history of horror cinema, had an enormous influence on the future of the genre. Never before had a horror film been the object of so much attention prior to its release, so much gossip about conflicts during post-production, so much speculation about why people of all ages stood in line for hours to see a work supposedly capable of inducing fits of vomiting, fainting, and even temporary psychosis. It is hard to convey the true cultural impact of The Exorcist. The film stole headlines from the Watergate scandal, at least for a while caused a considerable rise in the number of "real" cases of demonic possession and, as one critic wrote, "established grossness as a form of mass entertainment".

Inspired by newspaper reports about a 13-year-old Maryland boy whose body had supposedly been possessed by demonic forces, novelist William Peter Blatty turned the possessed boy into a girl. Blatty embellished many details, adding heavy doses of philosophical and theological speculation about the nature of evil, and the result was the 1971 book The Exorcist. Anticipating a bestseller, Warner Bros. bought the film rights, and after several revisions of the original screenplay, Blatty finally produced a version of The Exorcist that lived up to Friedkin's exacting standards.

In an era of student protests, experimental drug use, and the questioning of authority, The Exorcist let viewers revel in the horrific punishments inflicted on the rebellious Regan. But by making demon-Regan so fascinating to watch, so full of indecent surprises, The Exorcist also gave the audience the pleasure of rebellion. The film not only spawned a series of inferior sequels, imitations, and variations on the theme of possession, but also made children with evil powers a dominant theme in horror cinema.
content_list.credits: Summary based on the text by Steven Jay Schneider, published in the book 1001 Movies You Must See Before You Die

content_list.content_text: Brian De Palma (b. 1940) created a landmark (and one of the best adaptations to date of a Stephen King novel) with Carrie (1976). It was high-end horror for audiences who would rather have eaten their own foot than watch repulsive cannibal films or ghastly low-budget Italian productions.

information.contentText: A series of accidents occurred during the filming of "The Omen" when its original title was still "The Antichrist to the Birthmark." The hotel where director Richard Donner was staying was bombed by the IRA; screenwriter David Seltzer's plane had an accident; actor Gregory Peck canceled at the last minute a flight to Israel whose plane crashed, killing everyone on board; and the film's lead actors were also in a car accident on their way to shoot one of the film's scenes.

content_list.content_text: Horror blockbusters kept appearing throughout the 1980s, as studios softened the scares and added humor, special effects and fun. The result was family-friendly works such as Poltergeist (1982) and Ghostbusters (1984), which proved to be a good alternative to the repetitive, gory films that followed Halloween (1978).

In other cases, the advances in transformation effects achieved by Rick Baker (b. 1950) in An American Werewolf in London (1981) and by Rob Bottin (b. 1959) in The Thing (1982) showed that the splatter still mattered. A handful of smart, subversive horror films also appeared, among them The Fly (1986), seen by many as a commentary on the fear of the AIDS epidemic, and Clive Barker's (b. 1952) sadomasochistic fantasy Hellraiser (1987).
content_list.content_credits: Summary based on the text by Jamie Graham, published in the book "Cinema: The Whole Story" by Philip Kemp.

content_list.content_text: The girl runs deep into the woods, her clothes stained with the blood of her boyfriend, the football team's star, as well as of the group of friends who had decided to go camping for a few days. Behind her came the killer with a bloody machete and a mask covering his face. She was just one more victim of one more psychopath in one more slasher film that left its mark on the horror genre.
content_list.content_title: Slasher: the rise of a new horror subgenre

information.contentTitle: One of the Great Faces of Slasher Films
information.contentText: Although the term is sometimes used colloquially as a catch-all for any horror film involving murders, genre analysts cite an established set of characteristics that allegedly set these films apart from other horror subgenres, such as splatter films and psychological horror films.

content_list.content_text: Since its inception, cinema has always flirted with the fantastic and with fear. The first horror film is called Le manoir du diable (1896) and was directed by Georges Méliès (1861-1938); already at this early stage one notices a strong influence of the fantastic and the personification of an evil figure that tends to have the upper hand over the heroes. Along with the use of a menacing villain, it also became a rule to build a setting that did nothing to make the protagonists' lives easier, as can be seen in the aforementioned Méliès work and also in the Italian film L'inferno (Dante's Inferno, 1911), whose adaptation of Dante Alighieri's journey through the circles of hell featured a set design unique for its time, making skillful use of entirely new camera shots as well as illusionism and lighting techniques.

information.contentText: Because of the low budget, costumes and props were often created from items that were on hand or could be bought cheaply. Carpenter hired Tommy Lee Wallace as production designer, art director, location scout and co-editor. Wallace created the trademark mask worn by Michael Myers throughout the film from a Captain Kirk mask, bought for $1.98 at a costume store on Hollywood Boulevard. Carpenter recalled how Wallace "enlarged the eye holes and spray-painted the mask a bluish white. In the script it said Michael Myers' mask had 'the pale features of a human face' and it truly was spooky looking. I can only imagine the result if they hadn't painted the mask white." Hill adds that "the idea was to make him almost humorless and faceless — this sort of pale visage that could be human or not."

content_list.content_text: However, in the early 20th century, some filmmakers realized that the newborn horror genre didn't need to be tied to the fantastic. Just as small pamphlets about crimes were popular on English streets, German and French filmmakers experimented with adapting urban violence for the screen. From 1915 to 1916, Louis Feuillade's (1873-1925) film serial Les Vampires (The Vampires or, The Arch Criminals of Paris, 1915) set out to tell the story of a gang of house burglars in Paris who dressed as bats and stole jewelry, even committing a few murders.

The Italian subgenre known as giallo, in the 1960s and '70s, changed the entire aesthetic of what was understood by films involving murders. For the first time, a series of separate films established that there would be rules in a world of killings, rules that would become the basis for slasher films.

information.contentTitle: Scenes from A Nightmare on Elm Street
information.contentText: A Nightmare on Elm Street may have had its origins in director Wes Craven's childhood. The film's basic idea was inspired by several newspaper articles published in the LA Times in which the children of a group of Cambodian refugees, after taking refuge in the United States fleeing the Khmer Rouge regime, began having horrible nightmares, to the point of refusing to sleep. Following doctors' orders, the parents of these children encouraged them to sleep; however, each of them died in their sleep after another nightmare, and medical authorities at the time reported the phenomenon, calling it Asian Sudden Death Syndrome. On top of this, one night during Craven's childhood, he saw through the window of his house an old man walking outside who stopped and stared at him, then walked away; this incident frightened Craven badly and served as inspiration for the creation of Krueger.

content_list.content_text: The antagonist would be a mysterious killer whose clothing would give the audience little chance of guessing the culprit; his face would be covered by a mask; the camera shots would focus on his gloved hands during the act of murder; there would be a heroic figure embodied by a detective (amateur or not) who here represents law and order in the face of barbarism; and the killer's identity would only be revealed at the end.

quote.quote: There are horror films that deal with the psychological, the insinuating... and there are also those that bring the terrible horrors right up to your face, threatening to drench your body in sweat and lock your jaw shut forever. The Texas Chain Saw Massacre is one of those.
quote.author: Time Out London on The Texas Chain Saw Massacre (1975)

content_list.content_text: Director Mario Bava (1914-1980) released in 1963 the first example of the genre, La ragazza che sapeva troppo (The Girl Who Knew Too Much, 1963), a thriller in which a young American woman visits a friend in Rome and becomes an eyewitness to a murder, which culminates in an investigation she undertakes herself in search of the killer. The following year, Bava released Sei donne per l'assassino (Blood and Black Lace, 1964) and once again invoked the rule of a mysterious killer who piles up bodies over the course of the film.

information.contentText: Conceived and produced entirely over the course of about a year, the film was shot in Sydney Mines in the fall of 1980. It was released in theaters on February 11, 1981, by Paramount Pictures, coinciding with Valentine's Day. Despite a mixed critical response and a box office gross of US$5.7 million, the film has developed a large cult following over the years since its release.

content_list.content_text: It was then clear that the ground was ready for a new subgenre to emerge. The year 1974 became special for one filmmaker in particular. Tobe Hooper (1943-2017) had been an active member of the hippie movement in the '60s, and his first feature, Eggshells (1971), was well received for exploring the relationship of the youth of the time with drug use and sex, being regarded as a tribute to the end of the movement.

content_list.title: Halloween – The Landmark of Slasher Films
content_list.description:
No director since Alfred Hitchcock (1899-1980) has captured the delicious voyeurism of horror as well as John Carpenter does in Halloween, a film so full of our most primal anxieties that it still defines the genre 20 years later. Indeed, the comparison between Hitchcock and Carpenter is no exaggeration: Halloween is full of Carpenter's tributes to Hitchcock, from the characters' names - Sam Loomis and Tom Doyle, from Psycho (1960) and Rear Window (1954), respectively - to the casting of Jamie Lee Curtis (b. 1958), daughter of Janet Leigh (1927-2004), the unfortunate shower victim of Psycho.

Halloween's plot is quite simple: a masked psychopath, Michael Myers, stabs and strangles his way through a group of teenage friends as they drink beer and chase after sex, until he finally comes up against the film's great pure force, the virginal babysitter Laurie Strode (Curtis). Despite its minimalism, the evident social anxieties of good versus evil in Halloween's plot are left unresolved at the end, a strategy repeated consistently in other slashers ranging from Friday the 13th (1980) to Scream (1996). The intensity of Carpenter and of Debra Hill's (1950–2005) screenplay lies in placing horror in the placid setting of suburban American life, where young people are presumed (or at least were once presumed) to be safe.

Deconstructing the notion of the home as a protected place, Halloween's camerawork invades the fictional town of Haddonfield with a roaming point-of-view shot. The film opens with a brilliant shot showing everything through the eyes of the killer, then six years old. Carpenter builds a purely aesthetic fear, setting Halloween apart from its own tiresomely expository offspring. Throughout the film, someone is always watching, whether predator or prey. As the film unfolds, we find ourselves lurking around corners, behind shoulders, through windows and through cracks in closet doors, waiting for what we believe to be certain death.

The brilliant pacing and excruciatingly long takes keep the adrenaline high as Michael slinks through the shadows, cheating death several times to stalk the smart Laurie. When the film ends, we are left anxiously wondering what separates fact from fiction.
content_list.credits: Summary based on the text by Kathryn Bergeroo, published in the book 1001 Movies You Must See Before You Die

content_list.content_text: In '74, he released The Texas Chain Saw Massacre (1974) on a budget of US$300,000, earning a return of US$30,859,000, establishing not only an excellent financial return but also the rules for what would become the slasher, rules that were in turn inherited, with some modifications, from Mario Bava's giallo.

information.contentTitle: Scenes from The Texas Chain Saw Massacre
information.contentText: Hooper conceived the idea for the film after following the media coverage of ongoing acts of violence in the city of San Antonio, as well as the changes in the cultural and political landscape of the time; small plot details, such as the character Leatherface, were inspired by the crimes of serial killer Ed Gein (1906-1984). Most of the cast was made up of actors who were then unknown to the general public and had no previous film experience. The production of The Texas Chain Saw Massacre ran into several problems, such as the low budget, which forced the filmmaker to shoot long hours each day, seven days a week, so he could finish as quickly as possible and reduce equipment rental costs; the special effects were achieved in a simple, limited way. Because of the violent content, Hooper struggled to find a distributor; eventually, Louis Perano of Bryanston Pictures acquired the distribution rights. The filmmaker limited the amount of gore in the hope of ensuring the film would receive a PG rating (parental guidance suggested), but the Motion Picture Association of America (MPAA) rated it R (restricted).

content_list.content_text: The Texas Chain Saw Massacre defined the following rules: the serial killer would keep his identity secret. His methods of murder would not be limited to simply stabbing. The victims would be mostly young people constantly using drugs or having sex (the symbolism of lost purity and the punishment represented by the killer are very strong concepts in the early drafts of the Massacre screenplay), and the location of the murders would vary between isolated spaces, such as forests and farms, or urban ones, such as houses or schools. One of the victims would always survive at the end.

It was during the '70s that some of the best examples of the genre were produced, generating revenue and, consequently, more productions. Halloween (1978), by John Carpenter (b. 1948), would become established as one of the best horror films of the subgenre, with Michael Myers piling up bodies in Haddonfield.

information.contentText: At first, Friday the 13th was nothing more than a title. During the writing process, the project was called A Long Night at Camp Blood, but Cunningham believed in the potential of the name "Friday the 13th" and quickly placed an ad in Variety. Worried that someone owned the rights to the title, and in order to avoid potential lawsuits, Cunningham thought it best to look into it immediately. He hired a New York advertising agency to develop his concept for the film's logo, which consisted of large capital letters bursting through a pane of glass. In the end, Cunningham believed there were "no problems" with the title, but distributor George Mansour stated: "There was a movie before ours called Friday the 13th: The Orphan. It was moderately successful. But someone still threatened to sue. Phil Scuderi negotiated with them, and it was finally resolved."

content_list.content_text: Alice, Sweet Alice (1976) would feature one of the forerunners among cinema's serial killers to wear a stylized outfit (despite the obscurity into which the film fell), sporting a yellow raincoat and a translucent Halloween mask. Black Christmas (1974) would break some of the rules set by Massacre by setting its story inside a college sorority house, where a maniac who has escaped from an asylum hides inside the house, shattering the sense of everyday safety. When a Stranger Calls (1979) would bring back this concept in one of the most frightening opening sequences in history, which has also fallen into obscurity.

quote.quote: A summer-camp bogeyman story designed to do little more than build tension and deliver a few well-timed shocks, which it does with precision and even a bit of artistry.
quote.author: James Kendrick on Friday the 13th

content_list.content_text: Then came the '80s, and with them the heyday of the slasher subgenre, packing movie theaters and video stores with all kinds of stories that, despite oozing creativity in their kills and sometimes in their violence, increasingly lacked budget and therefore relied on weak casts and ever more amateurish productions.

information.contentText: Upon its release, Hellraiser divided critics but generally received praise; early reviews ranged from Melody Maker calling it the greatest horror film ever made in Britain to Roger Ebert condemning its "bankruptcy of imagination." It was followed by nine sequels, the first seven of which featured Bradley reprising his role as Pinhead.

content_list.content_text: The release of Friday the 13th (1980) introduced Jason Voorhees into the pantheon of great movie villains, followed to the letter the rules established by Massacre, and featured the special effects of Tom Savini (b. 1946), an absolute benchmark of the genre. In the wake of Friday the 13th came a flood of works that sought to copy its resounding success.

My Bloody Valentine (1981) brought the fearsome miner killing teenagers in every possible way with his pickaxe. Sleepaway Camp (1983) would offer a story along the lines of the Jason saga by setting a series of murders at a summer camp, but with the added bonus of one of the scariest endings in film history. Prom Night (1980) had as its premise a serial killer who hunts teenage victims at a school dance.

information.contentText: In the years since its release, Prom Night has gained a substantial cult following, not only for its horror content but also for its disco soundtrack, which was released by RCA Records in Japan in 1980. Some film scholars have cited it as one of the most influential horror films of the period.

content_list.content_text: A Nightmare on Elm Street (1984), by Wes Craven, would mark the debut of Freddy Krueger and his techniques for killing teenagers in their dreams. The glut of productions (and sequels to those productions) would lead to a resulting exhaustion of the subgenre, similar to what happened to Westerns in the middle of the 20th century.

quote.quote: I really think A Nightmare on Elm Street is one of the greatest fairy tales of any decade, because Craven understands the roots of those myths.
quote.author: Guillermo del Toro on A Nightmare on Elm Street (1984)

content_list.content_text: The '90s, however, held one last ace up the sleeve for the slasher when director Wes Craven (b. 1939) and screenwriter Kevin Williamson (b. 1965) teamed up and launched the Scream saga with Scream (1996). With the goal of rekindling audience interest in killer movies, Scream was born with the premise of not being a copy of formulas that had worked in the past and had worn these films out, but rather a non-comedic parody of the rules established by Mario Bava and Tobe Hooper.

information.contentText: As a young man, Brian De Palma, urged on by his mother, followed his father with recording equipment to try to catch him with another woman. This episode served as the inspiration for Dressed to Kill.

content_list.content_text: In other words, the story would not be comedic and would carry its own suspense, but it would constantly play with the conventions of the subgenre, such as the final girl, the killer's creative methods, stylized costumes, sexual morality, and so on. For a while, the success of Scream spurred the emergence of another franchise, I Know What You Did Last Summer (1997), which, lacking any originality, failed to replicate the success of Craven and Williamson's saga. Scream can also be considered the last great example of the slasher, which, despite sporadic works, has been losing ground to another subgenre, the haunting film.
content_list.content_credits: Summary based on the article "Slasher: a ascensão e queda de um subgênero" (Slasher: The Rise and Fall of a Subgenre), by Gustavo Barreto on rotacult.com.br.

movies.title: The Exorcist
movies.overview: 12-year-old Regan MacNeil begins to adapt an explicit new personality as strange events befall the local area of Georgetown. Her mother becomes torn between science and superstition in a desperate bid to save her daughter, and ultimately turns to her last hope: Father Damien Karras, a troubled priest who is struggling with his own faith.

movies.title: Halloween
movies.overview: On a black and unholy Halloween night years ago, little Michael Myers brutally slaughtered his sister in cold bold. But for the last fifteen years, town residents have rested easy, knowing that he was safely locked away in a mental hospital – until tonight. Tonight, Michael returns to the same quiet neighbourhood to relive his grisly murder again…and again…and again. For this is a night of evil. Tonight is Halloween!

movies.title: The Shining
movies.overview: Jack Torrance accepts a caretaker job at the Overlook Hotel, where he, along with his wife Wendy and their son Danny, must live isolated from the rest of the world for the winter. But they aren't prepared for the madness that lurks within.

movies.title: Carrie
movies.overview: Carrie White, a shy and troubled teenage girl who is tormented by her high school peers and her fanatically religious mother, begins to use her powers of telekinesis to exact revenge upon them.

movies.title: The Hills Have Eyes
movies.overview: On the way to California, a family has the misfortune to have their car break down in an area closed to the public, and inhabited by violent savages ready to attack.

movies.title: Night of the Living Dead
movies.overview: A group of people try to survive an attack of bloodthirsty zombies while trapped in a rural Pennsylvania farmhouse.

movies.title: Alien
movies.overview: During its return to the earth, commercial spaceship Nostromo intercepts a distress signal from a distant planet. When a three-member team of the crew discovers a chamber containing thousands of eggs on the planet, a creature inside one of the eggs attacks an explorer. The entire crew is unaware of the impending nightmare set to descend upon them when the alien parasite planted inside its unfortunate host is birthed.

movies.title: Child's Play
movies.overview: A single mother gives her son a beloved doll for his birthday, only to discover that it is possessed by the soul of a serial killer.

movies.title: A Nightmare on Elm Street
movies.overview: Teenagers in a small town are dropping like flies, apparently in the grip of mass hysteria causing their suicides. A cop's daughter, Nancy Thompson, traces the cause to child molester Fred Krueger, who was burned alive by angry parents many years before. Krueger has now come back in the dreams of his killers' children, claiming their lives as his revenge. Nancy and her boyfriend, Glen, must devise a plan to lure the monster out of the realm of nightmares and into the real world...

movies.title: The Omen
movies.overview: Immediately after their miscarriage, the US diplomat Robert Thorn adopts the newborn Damien without the knowledge of his wife. Yet what he doesn’t know is that their new son is the son of the devil.

movies.title: The Wicker Man
movies.overview: Police sergeant Neil Howie is called to an island village in search of a missing girl whom the locals claim never existed. Stranger still, however, are the rituals that take place there.

movies.title: Jaws
movies.overview: When an insatiable great white shark terrorizes the townspeople of Amity Island, the police chief, an oceanographer and a grizzled shark hunter seek to destroy the blood-thirsty beast.

movies.title: Black Christmas
movies.overview: A sorority house is terrorized by a stranger who makes frightening phone calls and then murders the sorority sisters during Christmas break.

movies.title: Poltergeist
movies.overview: Steve Freeling lives with his wife, Diane, and their three children, Dana, Robbie, and Carol Anne, in Southern California where he sells houses for the company that built the neighborhood. It starts with just a few odd occurrences, such as broken dishes and furniture moving around by itself. However, when he realizes that something truly evil haunts his home, Steve calls in a team of parapsychologists led by Dr. Lesh to help before it's too late.

movies.title: An American Werewolf in London
movies.overview: Two American tourists in England are attacked by a werewolf that none of the locals will admit exists.

movies.title: Hellraiser
movies.overview: An unfaithful wife encounters the zombie of her dead lover while the demonic cenobites are pursuing him after he escaped their sadomasochistic underworld.

movies.title: The Texas Chain Saw Massacre
movies.overview: When Sally hears that her grandfather's grave may have been vandalized, she and her paraplegic brother, Franklin, set out with their friends to investigate. After a detour to their family's old farmhouse, they discover a group of crazed, murderous outcasts living next door. As the group is attacked one by one by the chainsaw-wielding Leatherface, who wears a mask of human skin, the survivors must do everything they can to escape.

movies.title: Alice Sweet Alice
movies.overview: Alice is a withdrawn 12-year-old who lives with her mother and her younger sister, Karen, who gets most of the attention from her mother, leaving Alice out of the spotlight. When Karen is found brutally murdered in a church, suspicions start to turn toward Alice. But could a 12-year-old girl really be capable of such savagery?

movies.title: When a Stranger Calls
movies.overview: A psychopathic killer terrorizes a babysitter, then returns seven years later to menace her again.

movies.title: My Bloody Valentine
movies.overview: Twenty years ago in the sleepy mining town of Valentine Bluffs, a fatal mining disaster occurred on Valentine's Day while some of the crew was decorating for a party. The sole survivor of the accident killed the remaining crewmembers and warned the town not to celebrate Valentine's Day again. When a group of teenagers decides to defy that order, a murderous maniac in mining gear begins dispatching townsfolk in bloody and creative ways.

content_list.subtitle: The events that shaped the world
content_list.title: Timeline of Events from 1970 to 1989
content_list.description: The Exorcist is released, making audiences around the world sick and causing them to faint, creating a global hysteria. The first blockbuster is released: Jaws; meanwhile, auteur cinema grows with Martin Scorsese and other great directors. The '80s arrive with low-budget productions and era-defining comedies. Click here to see, in chronological order, the main events in cinema between 1940 and 1959.
